author: sjm41
body:
Hi @srengel @suzialeksander 

S. cerevisiae SER3 and SER33 have IDA, IMP and IGI annotation from  to GO:0061759 from PMID:26774271.

GO:0061759 is:
name: 2-oxoglutarate reductase activity
def: "Catalysis of the reaction: 2-oxoglutarate + reduced acceptor => (S)-2-hydroxyglutarate + acceptor." [PMID:26774271, RHEA:21254]

But quoting from PMID:26774271: "We also provide evidence that Ser3 and Ser33, which are primarily known for oxidizing 3-phosphoglycerate in the main serine biosynthesis pathway, in addition reduce α-ketoglutarate to D-2HG using NADH and represent major intracellular sources of D-2HG in yeast."

D-2HG corresponds to the R-enantiomer (not the S-enantiomer), so I think SER3 and SER33 should be annotated to the new GO term I just created in [#30833](https://github.com/geneontology/go-ontology/issues/30833) (when it's available):
+id: GO:0120568
+name: (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate (NAD+) dehydrogenase activity
+namespace: molecular_function
+def: "Catalysis of the reaction: (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate + NAD+ = 2-oxoglutarate + NADH + H+." [PMID:26774271, RHEA:49612]


That would then also match the RHEA/EC annotation for SER3/SER33 in UniProt:
https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P40054/entry
https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P40510/entry
title: S. cerevisiae SER3 and SER33 annotations to GO:0061759

author: ValWood
body:
Should we also remove "phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase activity"?

(R)-2-hydroxyglutarate (NAD+) dehydrogenase activity
appears to functionally replace the phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase in yeast.

author: srengel
body: should we remove it?  (S)-2-hydroxyglutarate and phosphoglycerate are not the same thing.

author: ValWood
body:
I think these annotations are IMP from
https://europepmc.org/article/MED/12525494

This is probably before it was known that yeast does this conversion slighty differently.
I was curious because I did not require " phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase in my model

I don't know if this is correct, but  this is what CHATGPT says:

This is one of those yeast annotation gotchas where reaction chemistry and physiological role don’t line up cleanly.
Here’s the precise reconciliation.
What SER3 (and SER33) actually do
Biochemically, Ser3 and Ser33 do not function as classical phosphoglycerate dehydrogenases in vivo.
Instead, they are best described as NAD⁺-dependent (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenases.
They catalyze:


(R)-2-hydroxyglutarate → 2-oxoglutarate
coupled to NAD⁺ → NADH

This reaction regenerates NAD⁺ locally.
So how do they support serine biosynthesis?
This is the clever yeast trick.

The “phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase step” in yeast is not a free-standing oxidation using soluble NAD⁺.
Instead, serine biosynthesis proceeds via a metabolite channeling / coupled reaction between:
Ser3/Ser33 (2-HG dehydrogenase activity)

Ser1 (phosphoserine aminotransferase)
In this system:
Ser1 produces 2-hydroxyglutarate as a byproduct when converting 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate to phosphoserine.

Ser3/Ser33 re-oxidize that 2-HG back to 2-oxoglutarate, regenerating NAD⁺.
The net effect is still oxidation of 3-phosphoglycerate → 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate, even though Ser3/33 never directly oxidize 3-PG.

So:
Annotation = correct: Ser3/Ser33 are (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenases.
Pathway role = PHGDH equivalent: they functionally replace phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase in yeast.
Why yeast does it this way

Avoids reliance on bulk cytosolic NAD⁺ availability
Allows tight coupling between carbon flux and redox balance
Explains why ser3Δ ser33Δ mutants block serine synthesis, even though no “canonical” PHGDH exists

Bottom line
Yeast do not have a classical PHGDH enzyme.
SER3/SER33 are redox partners that enable the PHGDH step indirectly.
If you want, I can sketch the reaction cycle explicitly (with intermediates and cofactors), or contrast this with how mammals and bacteria do the same step.


It might not be correct, but it seems too detailed and authoritative to be totally made up.

author: srengel
body:
i don't want to rely on chatgpt since its whole schtick is to produce plausible answers that sound detailed and authoritative while being totally made up.

remember this whole ticket is to change SER3 and SER33 from (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase to (S)-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase.

author: ValWood
body:
also 
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/302257v2.full.pdf

As described in a previous publication, while we could detect an NADH-dependent αketoglutarate (αKG) reductase activity (producing D-2-hydroxyglutarate) with the purified yeast Ser3
and Ser33 enzymes, detecting the presumed physiological activity (NAD-dependent oxidation of 3PGA)
proved much more difficult if not impossible [38]. 

This makes sense because the existing evidence is IMP. Its the same step via a different reaction.

author: srengel
body: oh good thx @ValWood for the PMID.  i have removed the phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase annotations from SER3 and SER33.  leaving only the (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate (NAD+) dehydrogenase annotation that @sjm41 requested.
